nodes.label: One definition of MOCK_API
nodes.rationale: MOCK_API is interpreted in exactly one module so both opt-in mechanisms (the withMock wrapper and the registry rewrite list) agree; a second implementation would let a fragment mock a route through one mechanism and not the other, which is indistinguishable from a bug in the route. Kept outside core/ because the flag is a host convention and core must stay importable by runtimes with no process.env. Mocking is hard-off when NODE_ENV=production: fabricated data reaching a real user is worse than a demo environment that cannot be mocked.

nodes.label: A mock nobody can see
nodes.rationale: A mocked endpoint that silently works is indistinguishable from a real one until the data is wrong, so every served request narrates itself: x-mock: 1 answers it in devtools, the [mock] line answers it in the terminal. Logging lives outside core/ for the same reason as the flag - writing to a console is a host convention and core is kept side-effect free so it can be used as a fixture factory. On by default; MOCK_LOG=0 silences it for verify suites where hundreds of generated responses would bury the assertions. Statuses >= 400 go to console.warn because a miss is the case worth spotting in a scrolling dev log.

nodes.label: Log line asserted as text
nodes.rationale: formatMockLog is split from logMock so the message a developer reads can be pinned without capturing a console; the feature is the text, not the fact that something was written somewhere.

nodes.label: mock/ is extractable as a package
nodes.rationale: The test travels with the code it constrains, unlike an eslint zone that lives in the host's config and will not move when the folder is lifted out - and a misconfigured rule fails silently. Concretely: no @/ alias, no path that resolves outside mock/, and core/ limited to zod, faker and (in tests) vitest, because the generator is the part with the widest reuse and its dependency list must not grow by accident.
nodes.norm_label: mock/ is extractable as a package

nodes.label: Registry public surface
nodes.rationale: types.ts is the vocabulary a host declares in, match.ts the pure key algebra, serve.ts the Request -> Response seam every adapter reuses. The table itself is host data passed in as an argument so the folder can be lifted into a package without dragging an application's endpoints with it. core/ is forbidden from importing any of this by an eslint zone: the registry knows what an HTTP route is, and the generator must not.

nodes.label: Most-specific-key-first ordering
nodes.rationale: Three tiebreaks - literal path beats dynamic, more query conditions beat fewer, exact value beats a binding - exist so that registering both of a pair does not make the winner depend on registry object key order, which is invisible in review and changes when someone sorts the table. The order mirrors how the App Router resolves property/search against property/[reference] and how a Next rewrite with a has condition is the narrower rule.

nodes.label: Malformed keys fail loudly
nodes.rationale: A key that is silently skipped produces a route that is simply never mocked, and the only symptom is real data arriving where fake data was expected - which reads as the flag not working. Duplicate bindings, empty values and catch-all segments are all rejected at parse time for the same reason; catch-alls additionally cannot be checked against the filesystem, which is the basis of the drift test.

nodes.label: The second platform-agnostic seam
nodes.rationale: handle() answers 'given this endpoint, what is the response?'; serveFromRegistry answers 'given this request, which endpoint?'. Every runtime that intercepts by path (Next, Playwright page.route, MSW, a Nest middleware) needs both and differs only in how it obtains a Request and hands back a Response, so none of them should re-implement key matching, the 404 cases or the schema thunk. The registry is always a parameter, never an import, because the table is host data and a library that reaches out for it cannot be lifted into a package.

nodes.label: Serve the caller's original URL
nodes.rationale: handle() seeds from hash(method + path + sorted query), so serving a rewritten path would silently return different data than the same request served through withMock. Reconstructing the request as the caller made it is each adapter's one real job.

nodes.label: Two-statement registry declaration
nodes.rationale: One annotation cannot both supply contextual types on the way in and read a concrete schema back out: annotating the thunk as () => Promise<z.ZodType> collapses the dynamic import's .then type parameter to z.ZodType, so every override check passes vacuously against unknown. So the draft type leaves schema untyped while typing options, and a second `satisfies CheckedMockRegistry<typeof registry>` statement reads each entry's real schema back up out of the literal. Two statements because the check must name the table's own type and a declaration cannot refer to itself.

nodes.label: Schema as a lazy thunk
nodes.rationale: An entry holds a function resolving a schema, never a schema value, so a build-time config (next.config.ts) can import the host's table to derive interception rules while reading only the keys - pulling in no application module, no zod and no faker. Laziness is runtime-only: TypeScript still resolves the dynamic import's type statically, which is what lets CheckedMockRegistry check overrides against the schema.

nodes.label: planned entry marker
nodes.rationale: A planned key is a design sketch for an endpoint that does not exist yet, so the drift test asserts it resolves to no route.ts; the day the real route lands the test fails and forces the entry to be promoted or deleted, which is what stops a stale mock silently shadowing a working endpoint.

nodes.label: Declaration next to the handler
nodes.rationale: withMock's advantage over the central table is that the declaration moves with the route file, so it cannot go stale when a route moves. It wraps the outside of auth wrappers, so a mocked route needs no session and reaches no backend. With the flag unset it returns the handler by identity - a production route is the exact function it was before, with no per-request work. A route declared in both mechanisms is a test failure, because the registry rewrite intercepts before the wrapper is reached and its options would be silently ignored.

nodes.label: Absent by resolution, not by flag
nodes.rationale: next.config.ts points turbopack.resolveAlias at index.prod.ts when NODE_ENV=production, so Turbopack never reads the real adapter and neither the generator nor faker can reach a chunk - the mock is absent by resolution rather than by a flag check the bundler must be clever enough to eliminate. Route sources are untouched. Every export of index.ts needs an assignment-compatible stub here, or tsc under a production-shaped build would disagree with the dev one; even an `import type` from core would re-introduce the reference this stub exists to avoid.
nodes.norm_label: absent by resolution, not by flag

nodes.label: Two Next entry points
nodes.rationale: withMock (wrapped around a handler) and serveRegistryRoute (behind a rewrite) both end in the same handle(). Build-time helpers are deliberately not re-exported: next.config.ts imports ./rewrites by relative path because Next's config loader does not resolve tsconfig path aliases, and because this barrel reaches the generator and faker, which config evaluation must not.

nodes.label: Thin-by-construction adapter
nodes.rationale: Matching, the 404 cases and the schema thunk all live in registry/serve.ts, which speaks Request/Response; what is left here is the two things only Next knows - how to recover the original URL from a rewrite and that a route must return a NextResponse. The isMockConfigured check is defence in depth: a production build emits no rewrite here, so reaching this route means someone requested /api/mock/... by hand. TODO(WP-412) notes the request body is not threaded through, which would diverge from the wrapper for POSTs.

nodes.label: Config-time emptiness in production
nodes.rationale: mockRewrites runs in plain Node at config time, before any bundling, and `next build` runs with NODE_ENV=production - so it returns an empty list and a production build contains no path to the mock endpoint at all: the feature is absent by construction rather than disabled by a runtime flag. Rewrites are beforeFiles so a registered route is intercepted before its route.ts is matched (afterFiles would never fire for a route that exists), one rule per unique path AND condition set since rewrites cannot match a method, emitted most-constrained-first because Next takes the first matching rule.

nodes.label: Next dialect stays in the adapter
nodes.rationale: A registry key is written the way the filesystem reads; Next wants :param in a source, a destination under the catch-all, and a directory under src/app/api for the drift test - all facts about the App Router, so none belong in mock/registry. The module imports registry/match directly rather than the barrel, because the index pulls in serve.ts and through it core and faker, and next.config.ts must stay cheap to evaluate. requireApiPath enforces the /api convention the destination algebra depends on, which the runtime-agnostic registry deliberately does not.
nodes.norm_label: next dialect stays in the adapter

nodes.label: Bindings become presence conditions
nodes.rationale: Next preserves the query string across a rewrite and serveFromRegistry re-matches the key at the destination, so asking Next to capture a binding would be a second, weaker copy of matching already done properly downstream. The gap is ?ref= (present but empty), which satisfies presence and is then rejected by matchQuery - an explicit 404 rather than a fall-through, the right trade since a page about the empty string is the failure nobody would look for. Exact values are regex-escaped because Next compiles `value` to a regex and an unescaped dot would match any character.

nodes.label: Query must never reach a rewrite source
nodes.rationale: A key's query string handed to a rewrite `source` is `Unexpected MODIFIER` from path-to-regexp - a build-time failure that takes the dev server down - because source is a path grammar knowing nothing about ? or [...]. Query conditions belong in the separate has array, and these tests pin that split plus the ordering it forces, which no type can express.
nodes.norm_label: query must never reach a rewrite source
